Introduction:
Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are a major public health issue, responsible for 74% of global deaths, with 77% of all NCD mortality occurring in low- and middle-income countries [ 1 ]. Cardiovascular disease (CVD), cancers, chronic respiratory disease (CRD), and diabetes are regarded as major NCDs, affecting most of the population aged 30–69 years [ 1 ]. These conditions often require long-term, sometimes lifelong, treatment and follow-up to maintain the health status of patients. Disruption in access to routine healthcare services for their management may increase morbidity and mortality, affecting the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG 3) of ensuring healthy lives and minimizing premature deaths due to NCDs.

In late December 2019, a novel coronavirus disease emerged in China and had spread to >77 countries by March 2020. The World Health Organization identified this disease as COVID-19 and declared it a pandemic [ 2 , 3 ]. In response, most nations instituted strict controls, including lockdowns, social isolation, and travel restrictions (isolations and quarantine), anticipating its quick spread. These measures led to partial or complete disruption of preventive, curative, and rehabilitative services for NCDs and other health issues [ 3 ]. The disruption had a serious effect in low-income countries, which already had limited capacity and where people had limited access to affordable, quality care [ 4–6 ]. Management of the pandemic itself necessitated ad hoc changes to meet the surge in patient volumes, including the suspension of routine primary health services, cancellation of scheduled treatments, and the reallocation of healthcare resources and personnel to COVID-19 wards [ 7 ]. These adaptations, compounded by the unavailability of public transportation induced by lockdown measures, further exacerbated access limitations to essential health services during the crisis. Furthermore, lockdowns caused economic losses, making it harder for patients to pay for and use services [ 5 , 6 , 8 ], thus reducing their follow-up visits and medication adherence [ 9 ]. In addition to these factors, public fear of infection and the stigma associated with infected or suspected cases have resulted in a decrease in healthcare utilization, particularly for routine, elective, and preventive visits [ 4 , 5 ].

The consequences of limiting access to preventive and therapeutic services for NCDs—including increased mortality, poor mental health, and post-lockdown effects on chronic diseases—due to strict pandemic measures have been widely discussed in the literature [ 4 , 5 , 7 , 8 , 10 ]. However, evidence from low- and middle-income countries, which were disproportionately affected by the pandemic and subsequent stringent control measures including lockdowns, remains underexplored. Nepal, a low-income country with limited healthcare resources, implemented a nationwide lockdown from 24 March to 14 August 2020, restricting all kinds of travel and border closure. The healthcare, already grappling with challenges such as poverty, illiteracy, inadequate infrastructure, shortage of trained professionals, cultural barriers, political instabilities, and geographical obstacles to providing quality care, experienced further compromises in service delivery [ 11 , 12 ]. These limitations were reflected in increased mortality and morbidity indicators for NCDs—mainly CVD, CRD, cancer, hypertension (HTN), and chronic kidney disease (CKD) [ 4 ]. In Nepal, deaths from amendable causes—such as hypertensive diseases, diabetes mellitus, kidney disease, and other conditions—have been rising, accounting for about two-thirds of total deaths in 2015 [ 13 ]. While mortality and morbidity are influenced by multiple factors, many of which lie outside the healthcare system, access to high-quality healthcare services remains crucial for managing and preventing these amendable NCD-related deaths [ 14 , 15 ]. Meanwhile, a systematic assessment of these impacts in Nepal in relation to health service disruption attributed to stringent containment measures remains unavailable. We therefore aimed to analyse the effects on services for CVD, CRD, cancer, HTN, and CKD by using a robust epidemiological design, controlling for time-invariant confounders, long-term trends, and the seasonality of selected NCDs.
Methods:
We conducted interrupted time series (ITS) analysis by using monthly counts of outpatient department visits for selected NCDs (CVD, CRD, cancer, HTN, and CKD) to evaluate the impacts of lockdown on health service utilization after controlling for time-invariant confounders, seasonality, and long-term trend affecting the population-level distribution of these diseases [ 16 , 17 ]. We used the reference period of lockdown implementation from March 2020 to August 2020 as the primary intervention period to assess the situation during the COVID-19 pandemic. The main health outcomes in this study were outpatient department visits for CVD (cerebrovascular and coronary heart diseases), CRD, cancer, HTN, and CKD, and the utilization of free services for patients with selected NCDs. The database we used defines CVD as including the following heart-related conditions: ischemic heart disease, vascular heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, cardiac arrest, heart failure, congestive heart failure, stroke, and other cardiac-related conditions [ 18 , 19 ]. HTN is both a non-communicable disease and a major metabolic risk factor for cardiovascular and kidney diseases. In our source datasets, these conditions were recorded separately; therefore, we analysed them independently. The free health service scheme, implemented by the Nepal government, aims to provide financial relief to individuals facing severe and financially burdensome diseases such as CVD, cancer, renal failure, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, head and spinal injury, sickle cell anemia, and stroke. For this study, we have included data of patients receiving free health services for selected CVD (defined earlier), CKD, and cancer only. We evaluated the impact of lockdown by estimating the percentage change in the number of outpatient department visits and the utilization of free services as the function of intervention implementation.

### Data collection and management

The observation period spanned 33 months, from July 2018 to April 2021 (corresponding to the Nepali calendar dates of Shrawan 1, 2075 to Chaitra 30, 2077), encompassing 20 months before and 13 months after the lockdown implementation. Monthly data on outpatient department visits for patients with NCDs were retrieved from the Integrated Health Information Management Section (IHIMS), Department of Health Services of the Ministry of Health and Population (MoHP), Nepal. The IHIMS, under the Policy, Planning, and Monitoring Division of Nepal’s Department of Health Services, manages routine health data from the ward level, the smallest administrative unit, to the federal level through predefined processes [ 20 ]. It collects, verifies, and processes data from both the public and private sectors to maintain a centralized data bank. The Department of Health Services publishes the annual health report by using data generated by IHIMS [ 19 ]. As the annual report and data are published at the end of the fiscal year, we were unable to obtain additional data for analysis. Data were then checked for duplication and inconsistencies by using Microsoft Excel before being imported into R-software for further analysis. COVID-19 data were extracted from daily reports published by MoHP and imported into Excel 2010.

### Statistical analysis

We used descriptive statistics to summarize the number of monthly hospital visits for selected NCDs, namely CRD, CVD, cancer, CKD, and HTN. We utilized a scatterplot of the time series to illustrate the outpatient department visits for selected NCDs before and after the lockdown period. The association between hospital outpatient department visits and lockdown implementation was estimated by using a quasi-Poisson regression model to account for overdispersion. We controlled the models for seasonality by using Fourier terms, incorporated an indicator variable for the time to control long-term effect, and included a 1-month lag of residuals in the model to control residual autocorrelation. The final model to compute the acute effect of lockdown on health service utilization was defined by using the following equation:

In this model, y t represents the outpatient department visits of each selected NCD patient at time t ; β 0 is the intercept; exp ( β 1 ) denotes the change in outpatient department visits with respect to the change in unit time; exp ( β 2 ) indicates the change in number of outpatient department visits during lockdown period; and β 3 indicates the slope of change following the intervention (interaction between time and intervention). Fourier terms were determined by using Quasi-Akaike Information Criterion. The intervention start point was defined as 25 March 2020, when the government of Nepal officially announced the lockdown. The pre-intervention period spanned from mid-July 2018 to mid-March 2020 ( T = 1 to T = 20) and the post-intervention period was from 25 March 2020 to 13 June 2021 ( T = 21 to T = 33), encompassing 20 months pre intervention and 13 months post intervention.

The estimated percentage of immediate change and the average annual change in the secular trend were calculated by using the coefficient of the lockdown indicator ( β 2 ) and the interaction term between time and the lockdown indicator ( β 3 ) in the model, respectively. We calculated the number of averted outpatient department visits by subtracting the actual outpatient department visits from the predicted number without the influence of the lockdown.

We tested the model fit by plotting residuals, autocorrelation functions, and partial autocorrelation functions. All statistical tests were two-sided and a P -value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed by using R v4.0.1 ( http://www.R-project.org ). All data analyses were conducted in 2022.
Results:
This study analysed the outpatient department visits and the utilization of free services for selected NCDs by using data retrieved from IHIMS, Nepal. A total of 3 985  500 outpatient department visits were recorded in the 20 months before the COVID-19 pandemic compared with 2 745  395 visits during the pandemic, indicating an overall 31.1% reduction in outpatient department visits, as shown in Table 1 . Similarly, the utilization of free services decreased by 12.5%, from 51 054 cases pre pandemic to 44 661 cases post pandemic. Among individual NCD categories, the major decline in outpatient department visits was observed for cancer (50.2%), followed by CVD (45.2%) and CRD (32.6%). CKD and HTN experienced smaller declines of 16.7% and 27.5%, respectively. Free service utilization also declined, with the largest reductions seen in CVD (37.8%) and CKD (19.9%), while cancer services experienced a relatively smaller decrease of 6.7%.

Figure 1 illustrates trends in outpatient department visits for patients with chronic NCDs before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. CRD and HTN consistently accounted for the highest number of outpatient department visits, showing a sharp decline after the onset of lockdown in March 2020, followed by a gradual but incomplete recovery. CVD and CKD exhibited similar patterns, showing significant drops post lockdown and slower recovery rates. Cancer visits were the least frequent and showed the most substantial decline, with minimal rebound.

Figure 2 shows an ITS analysis of monthly outpatient department visits for patients with NCDs. The graph compares the expected number of outpatient department visits for each NCD during the post-lockdown period to the observed number of outpatient department visits. The grayed-out area on the white background reflects the period of the COVID-19 pandemic. The figure demonstrates that, after lockdown, there was a dramatic decrease in the rate of outpatient department visits by all studied NCDs, including cancer, CRD, HTN, CVD, and CKD. While the expected and observed lines for CRD, CKD, and HTN are almost parallel, those for CVD and cancer appear to be slightly out of alignment. The slope of the outpatient department visit rate before and after the lockdown appears to be similar, indicating that the lockdown caused an immediate drop in outpatient department visits, but that the rise in outpatient department visits has followed the same trajectory as before.

The results for the effect of the lockdown are summarized in Table 2 , reporting the relative risk (RR) when comparing the periods before and after lockdown. The model shows evidence that the COVID-19 pandemic has affected outpatient department visits for cancer and CVD. There was a 73% [RR 0.27, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.089–0.808] decrease in outpatient department visits for CVD and a 64% (RR 0.36, 95% CI: 0.175–0.745) decrease in outpatient department visit for cancer patients. Though an immediate reduction in outpatient department visits was observed, the model lacks adequate evidence to show the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on outpatient department visits for CRD (RR 0.89, 95% CI: 0.651–1.228), HTN (RR: 1.004, 95% CI: 0.64–1.575), and CKD (RR 0.589, 95% CI: 0.231–1.501). This signifies that outpatient department visits for HTN, CRD, and CKD remained almost constant before and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Figure 3 shows the trend of services utilization under the free health service scheme by patients for major NCDs (CVD, CKD, and cancer) before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. The number of patients utilizing services for CKD remained relatively high and did not show a significant decline during the COVID-19 waves; there was consistently high utilization, even during the COVID-19 periods, which might have been due to the requirement for the continuity of care for CKD such as dialysis. The utilization of services for heart disease and cancer declined during the COVID-19 periods.

Figure 4 shows an ITS analysis of the monthly utilization of free health services for NCDs. The graph compares the expected numbers for service utilization for each NCD during the post - lockdown period to the observed numbers for service utilization. The grayed-out area on the white background reflects the period of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Though an immediate reduction in the utilization of free services was observed, Table 3 shows that the model lacks adequate evidence to show the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on the utilization of free services for cancer (RR 1.76, 95% CI: 0.45–7.05), CVD (RR 0.37, 95% CI: 0.06–2.11), and kidney disease (RR 1.45, 95% CI: 0.69–3.01).
Discussion:
This study reveals a notable decline in the number of outpatient department visits and the utilization of free healthcare services for NCDs immediately following the COVID-19 lockdown in Nepal. The data strongly suggest a significant impact of the lockdown on outpatient department visits for cancer and CVD. Specifically, there was a marked reduction in visits for these conditions, indicating that the lockdown had a substantial effect on healthcare access and utilization for these diseases.

We also observed a decrease in outpatient visits for CRD, HTN, and CKD; however, the statistical evidence was insufficient to definitively attribute these changes to the lockdown. While trends in the utilization of free services for cancer, CKD, and CVD showed variations before and after the lockdown, none of these changes was statistically significant. This lack of significance suggests that the observed differences might be attributed to random variation rather than a definitive effect of the lockdown on service utilization.

Our findings are consistent with a systematic review of 17 cancer studies and 14 cardiovascular studies that were conducted primarily in the region of Southeast Asia, which reported a 30%–40% reduction in outpatient department services during the pandemic [ 21 ]. Additionally, a study conducted across multiple hospitals in India also observed decreased hospital visits and treatment for NCDs during the pandemic, despite having adequate resources and infrastructure [ 22 ]. This aligns with our findings, highlighting that, even in countries with well-established healthcare systems, outpatient department visits and service utilization for NCDs were significantly affected by the pandemic. In contrast, a time - series analysis from China reported a reduction in hospital visits for respiratory diseases, but found no significant effect on outpatient department visits for CVD [ 23 ]. Although our study found no significant impact on service utilization for NCDs, the general trend of reduced service utilization during the pandemic is consistent with those of other reviews and studies. These have shown reductions in all aspects of NCD care, including screening, diagnosis, treatment, palliative care, and follow-up management [ 21 ]. Similar findings from retrospective studies in Croatia and China attributed reductions in hospital and outpatient services to factors such as lockdowns, the reorganization of hospital operations, the rationing of medical resources, and public reluctance to seek care due to infection risks [ 11 , 12 ]. These factors likely contributed to decreased access to services and travel restrictions during the pandemic.

Given the essential role of primary care in the prevention and management of NCDs, the impact of the pandemic on healthcare access has exacerbated challenges in managing these chronic conditions. Regular follow-ups and adherence to medication are crucial for managing NCDs effectively. The disruption in these services underscores the need for continuity of care as part of pandemic preparedness, ensuring that chronic conditions are managed appropriately despite public health measures and the direct impacts of the pandemic [ 24 ].
Strengths and limitations: Our study has several strengths, including a robust quasi-experimental design that effectively teases out the association between lockdown enforcement and the disruption of healthcare service utilization nationwide by using official data from the IHIMS, MoHP. However, this study has several limitations. First, the analysis was conducted at an aggregate level rather than on an individual basis, and it only covers the first lockdown phase. Second, we assumed lockdown implementation as a discrete, point-in-time intervention rather than an intervention period over a period of time. This assumption may oversimplify the nature of the lockdown, potentially underestimating or misrepresenting gradual or phase effects that occurred throughout the enforcement period. Consequently, the observed changes in healthcare service utilization may not fully account for varying levels of lockdown stringency or compliance over time. A sequential analysis that includes all pandemic waves would offer a clearer picture of the overall impact. Further research is needed to evaluate the long-term effects of these disruptions on patient outcomes.
Conclusion: The COVID-19 pandemic reduced outpatient department visits and utilization of free health services for NCDs, especially cancer and CVD. The lockdown likely disrupted medication adherence and physical activity, potentially leading to complications and advanced disease stages. These reductions in service access may have resulted in delayed diagnoses and suboptimal treatment. It is crucial for the health system to maintain continuous care for NCD patients during pandemics.
